newsitem.title: USA: Clinton calls for doubling of adoptions by 2002.
newsitem.headline: Clinton calls for doubling of adoptions by 2002.

text.p: President Clinton Saturday directed his Cabinet to launch an all-out effort to double the number of children adopted by 2002, while ruling out adopting a child of his own for the time being.

"The holidays we celebrate this month teach us that through faith and love we can truly repair the world," Clinton said in his weekly radio address. "I can think of no better way to fulfil the promise of this season than to bring a child into a family, and a family to a child.

At the same time, the White House said Clinton and his wife Hillary had decided against adopting a child while they are in the White House because they believed they would not be able to devote the kind of attention the child would need.

A spokesman, Barry Toiv, said Clinton in a number of pre-Christmas interviews, not yet published or aired, had said that "he didn't rule it out for later in life but he basically said it wouldn't work here in the White House."

In a May interview with Time magazine, Mrs. Clinton said she and her husband had discussed the possibility of adopting. They have one child, Chelsea, 16. Mrs. Clinton ignored a question about the possibility of adoption at the radio address event.

The event in the Oval Office had a poignant touch. As Clinton spoke, he and Mrs. Clinton were surrounded by a number of adopted children, their foster parents, and several children awaiting adoption. They all chatted afterward.
"My brother got adopted and hopefully I'll get adopted by the same family," said a 13-year-old boy identified only as Daniel, sitting at Clinton's feet.

In his remarks, Clinton said there are more than 450,000 children in the country's foster care system, located there because of abuse, neglect or a home life neither safe nor secure. Most will return home eventually but the government predicts 100,000 of them will not.
"Those children wait far too long, typically three years or more, to find permanent homes and families to love them," he said.

Earlier this year Clinton and Congress moved to try to speed up adoptions by approving a $5,000 tax credit to help families who adopt children. A law he signed also prohibited adoption agencies from denying or delaying placement of a waiting child based on race, colour or national origin.

Clinton said he signed a directive ordering Health and Human Services Secretary Donna Shalala to launch an extensive effort to determine what steps are needed to meet the goal of at least doubling by 2002 the number of children in foster care who are adopted or permanently placed each year.
"We will double the number of children we move from foster care to permanent homes, from 27,000 a year today, to 54,000 a year by the year 2002," he said.

He told Shalala to report back in 60 days. He said her report should include how to help states set and meet new adoption targets and must describe how to improve coordination among local, state and federal authorities so every community has access to the best ways to encourage adoption.
Clinton said the effort must also outline "sensible financial incentives" to provide states to raise adoption rates.
Meantime, he instructed the departments of Treasury, Labour, Commerce as well as HHS to launch an "all-out effort" to heighten public awareness about adoption.

"We must work tirelessly to make sure that every boy and girl in America who is up for adoption, has a family waiting out to reach to him or her. No child should be in foster care for one day longer than he or she needs to be," he said.
